single_run.intro_content: Here you run ComFy on one event log: it discovers Petri nets with the chosen miners and computes their complexity measures. The page has three sections: the log, the miners and measures, and the run. Esc or Skip ends the tour at any time.
single_run.logsource_content: Two sources: “Upload file” for your own XES or JSON file (recent uploads and the logs of your datasets are listed below), or “Use example” for the bundled example log. The overview shows what is in the log.
single_run.params_content: Choose the miners to run and the measures to compute. The preset bar above saves a selection for later.
single_run.run_content: Start with the button or Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on a Mac). The result appears below with the measures, the discovered nets and downloads; the run is listed in the History.

onboarding.step0_p1: Find out which complexity measures of process models and event logs capture the same thing. Load or compute a table of measures, check whether it suits a factor analysis, and read off groups of related measures.
onboarding.step0_p2: This quick tour shows the four things you'll use most.
onboarding.step1_p1: Model complexity analyses measures of Petri nets discovered from event logs, computed with ComFy. Log complexity analyses measures of the event logs themselves, computed with feeed.
onboarding.step1_p2: Both tabs work the same way.
onboarding.step2_p1: Data, dataset, suitability, factors, loadings: the list of steps shows what each one found and opens it; Back and Next lead through them. Every change to a setting re-runs the analysis right away, and the analysis can be downloaded as CSV, LaTeX or ZIP. An optional sixth step lets Claude propose names for the factors.
onboarding.step2_p2: Hover a control or an (i) for what it does; the Tour button walks you through the steps.
onboarding.step3_compare: Compare: the factor structures of several analyses side by side, like Tab. 17 of Important Factors.
onboarding.step3_history: History: every dataset and run of your session.
onboarding.step3_inspect: Single log: run ComFy on one log and look at the discovered models.

factor.intro: Five steps from raw measures to factors, and an optional interpretation, one at a time: the list of steps on the left (on a phone the row at the top) and Back and Next move between them. Hover a control or an (i) for what it does. Esc or Skip ends the tour at any time.
factor.data: Where the data come from: Get started and the bundled datasets, a CSV of your own, or measures computed from your files. Large computations run in the background.
factor.dataset: Check the size of the matrix and what the cleaning removed. You can download the cleaned data as CSV.
factor.suitability: Bartlett and KMO tell you whether a factor analysis makes sense at all. Exclude measures with low MSA here, by hand or with the filter.
factor.factors: The scree plot suggests how many factors to keep. Change the number or the rotation; everything below updates right away.
factor.loadings: The heatmap shows which measures load on which factor; bold values reach the threshold. Export the table as CSV or LaTeX for your paper.
factor.interpretation: Optional: Claude proposes a name and a short reading for each factor. Only the measure names, their definitions and aggregated results are sent, and every request costs money, so it runs only when you press the button. Always check it against the loadings.

stability.help: Draws {n} bootstrap samples of the rows, with replacement and a fixed seed, and fits each with the same measures, factor count and rotation. Tucker's congruence φ with the Hungarian algorithm matches the factors of a sample to these, mirrored where φ is negative; then the same assignment rule applies. The value of a measure is the share of samples in which it keeps its factors.
stability.heywood: In {n} samples a further measure reached the Heywood bound; they are kept.
stability.none_valid: None of the {samples} samples could be fitted.
stability.stale: The stability shown before belongs to other settings.
stability.failed: The stability could not be computed.
stability.value_tip: Same factors in {pct} of the samples
stability.phi_tip: Mean congruence with the matching factor of the samples; 5th percentile {p5}.
stability.pairs_label: Pairs of measures over the samples
stability.pairs_legend_short: Share of the samples in which two measures share a factor
stability.pairs_legend: Each cell is the share of the valid samples in which the two measures share at least one factor; the darker, the more often. A ring marks the pairs that share a factor in the solution itself.
stability.pairs_cell_more: Share a factor in {pct} of the samples
stability.pairs_cell_together: Share a factor in {pct} of the samples; together in the solution

short_set.badge_tip: Represents this dimension in the short set: purity {purity}
short_set.heading: Short set ({n} measure)
short_set.help: One measure per dimension: the one assigned to it with the highest purity, its absolute loading on the dimension minus its largest absolute loading on any other. It lets you report a few measures that do not repeat each other, as the Important Factors paper motivates. Ties go to the higher loading. A representative with a low stability should be read with care.

help.cleaning: Before the analysis, rows where most values are missing are dropped. Then columns that are not numeric, that have no variance, that have missing values, or that are perfect copies of an earlier column are removed, as in ComFy for log measures. Such columns would distort or break the correlation matrix.
help.bartlett: Bartlett's test checks the null hypothesis that the correlation matrix is an identity matrix, i.e. that the measures are uncorrelated. If p < α, there are correlations that common factors can explain. With many observations the test almost always passes, so read it together with KMO.
help.kmo: The Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin criterion compares the correlations between the measures with their partial correlations. Values near 1 mean the measures share common variance; values near 0 mean the correlations are mostly pairwise. Kaiser's scale (Kaiser 1974): from 0.9 marvelous, 0.8 meritorious, 0.7 middling, 0.6 mediocre, 0.5 miserable, below that unacceptable.
help.msa: The measure of sampling adequacy (MSA) is the KMO value of a single measure. A measure with low MSA shares little with the others and fits no common factor well; removing it usually raises the overall KMO. Tick a measure to exclude it by hand.
help.msa_filter: As in ComFy, all measures below the threshold are removed and the MSA values are recomputed, until every remaining measure reaches the threshold. If the overall MSA then lies below the threshold, ComFy ends its run; the tool only warns.
help.msa_threshold: The filter removes measures whose MSA is below this value, and the overall KMO counts as adequate from this value on. ComFy and ComFy for log measures use 0.6.
help.bartlett_alpha: The significance level of Bartlett's test: the test passes when p is below α. ComFy and ComFy for log measures use 0.05.
help.scree: The scree plot shows the eigenvalues of the correlation matrix in descending order. Look for the elbow where the curve flattens; factors after it add little. The elbow, the eigenvalue-above-1 rule and the parallel analysis can disagree, so treat them as starting points. The thin line on the right axis adds up the eigenvalues: the share of the variance the first principal components explain. The factors of the analysis explain somewhat less, as step 5 shows.
help.eigenvalue: An eigenvalue belongs to a principal component of the correlation matrix: the variance it explains, in units of one standardized measure. The suggestion keeps as many factors as there are eigenvalues above 1 (Kaiser criterion), i.e. as many as there are components that explain more than a single measure.
help.rotation: Rotation turns the factor solution so that each measure loads strongly on as few factors as possible, which makes the factors easier to name. It does not change how much variance the factors explain together. Varimax and quartimax keep the factors uncorrelated; promax and oblimin let them correlate.
help.threshold: Loadings with an absolute value at or above this threshold count as substantial. Which factors a measure joins depends on the assignment rule above; with the largest loading, it joins the factor where its absolute loading is highest, if that loading reaches the threshold. Common choices lie between 0.3 and 0.5; ComFy uses 0.35, ComFy for log measures 0.5. Whether a loading exactly on the threshold counts depends on the rule: with the largest loading it counts (≥); ComFy's report, which only greys loadings below its threshold, leaves it black as well. The rules of Important Factors (multiple membership, Hair) require more than the threshold (>), as the tables of the paper do.
help.loading: A loading says how strongly a measure goes along with a factor. For orthogonal rotations it is the correlation between measure and factor. For oblique rotations the pattern matrix holds regression weights and the structure matrix the correlations. The sign gives the direction: measures with opposite signs on the same factor move in opposite directions.
help.communality: The communality h² is the share of a measure's variance that all kept factors explain together. A low value (below about 0.4) means the factors do not capture the measure well.
help.variance: SS loadings is the sum of squared loadings of a factor. Divided by the number of measures it gives the proportion of the total variance the factor explains; the cumulative row adds these up.
help.groups: Each factor with the measures assigned to it, strongest loading first. Measures in one group capture a similar aspect of complexity; the name of the factor is up to your interpretation. Under multiple membership a measure can be in several groups; a chip names its other factors.
help.communality_threshold: Measures whose communality is below this value are left unassigned, because the factors explain too little of them. ComFy for log measures uses 0.5; 0 keeps every measure, except under multiple membership (at least 0.3) and Hair (at least 0.5).
help.factor_correlations: With an oblique rotation the factors may correlate. Values near 0 mean the factors are nearly independent; large values mean they measure related aspects.
help.assignment: How the loadings turn into factor groups. The largest loading is the default of this tool: each measure joins the factor it loads on most. ComFy's report assigns nothing; it only greys loadings with |λ| below its threshold. Important Factors states two further rules: for Tab. 6–16, a measure also joins every factor whose loading is at most {gap} below its largest (multiple membership), with h² ≥ {h2_multi}; for Tab. 17, it follows Hair et al. with h² ≥ {h2_hair} and leaves cross-loaded measures out. The tool applies the rules as stated; where a table of the paper differs from them, a note below the rules says so for the bundled datasets. The factor solution is the same under every rule; only the groups change.
help.criteria: Kaiser keeps every factor with an eigenvalue above 1. Parallel analysis (Horn) keeps the factors whose eigenvalue is above the {percentile}th percentile of the eigenvalues of {simulations} random normal datasets of the same size, computed on principal components with the fixed seed {seed}; with many observations it comes close to Kaiser. A paper may also fix the number before the analysis. Choosing a criterion sets the number of factors.

interpretation.intro: Claude reads the loadings together with the definitions of the measures and proposes a name and a short interpretation for each factor. Sent to Anthropic are the measure (column) names, their catalog definitions and aggregated results such as loadings and test statistics; measure values, row labels and file names are not sent. Each request costs money, so it runs only when you ask for it.

guide.title: User guide
guide.subtitle: What {app} does, step by step: analyse a published dataset or your own data, read the results, and take them into a paper.

links.paper: Open Important Factors: Inductive miner with the paper settings
links.compare: Compare the four miners of Tab. 17

steps.title: The six steps
steps.p1: Model complexity analyses the measures of ComFy on Petri nets, Log complexity the measures of feeed on event logs. Both walk through the same steps: Data, Dataset, Suitability, Factors, Loadings and an optional Interpretation. One step is on screen at a time; the list of steps shows what each step found.
steps.p2: The settings row above the steps sums up every choice, marks those that differ from the tool standard and leads to each control. Every change of a setting runs the analysis again.
steps.p3: The tabs at the top are the same on every page: the analyses (the two of complexity and Single log), and set apart on the right the tools Compare and History. The guide and the settings are in the header and lead back to the tab you came from.

bundled.title: Analyse a published dataset

items.open: Open Model complexity or Log complexity.
items.choose: In Data, choose a dataset of a paper, for example Important Factors: Inductive miner.
items.settings: Choose Paper settings to analyse it as the paper did, or Tool standard for the defaults of ComFy, then Load dataset. The data step stays on screen with what was loaded and the way on.

bundled.p1: With the paper settings, a chip in the settings row says whether the numbers equal the published ComFy report and how the tables of the paper relate to it. Get started, the first cards of the bundled datasets in the data step, loads such an analysis in one click; View result then opens its loadings.

own.title: Analyse your own data

items.logs: Event logs (.xes, .xes.gz): for model measures, every log is mined with every miner you choose and every net is measured; for log measures, feeed computes the feature groups you choose. Unfold a group to choose single measures of it, so that a few logs can carry a few measures; below the choice the data step says how many observations and measures that gives, and when there are too few for a factor analysis.
items.nets: Petri nets (.pnml): every net is measured.
items.csv: A CSV file: one row per observation, one column per measure; a first column of names becomes the row labels.

own.p2: Logs and nets are computed in a job. The tab History says what runs (“1 running · 37%”) and has a red dot for a failed run you have not seen yet; a dataset that has been computed raises a notice “… is ready · Open” wherever you are. My datasets, a source of the data step, reopens a dataset of the session with the settings of its last analysis.
own.p3: A dataset of nets from several miners has a row per log and miner. The dataset step offers all miners together or one miner at a time, as Important Factors analyses them: together, the differences between the miners mix into the dimensions and each log counts once per miner; one miner has fewer observations. A miner with no more observations than measures cannot be analysed; below five per measure the analysis warns. Compare the miners there opens their factor structures side by side.
own.p4: A row of a dataset computed from logs has a View this log link in the dataset step. It opens the page Inspect a single log with that log and, for a row of nets, only the miner of the row chosen, as long as the log is among the ten newest uploads of the session; the page says when it is not.
own.p5: History lists everything of the session, newest first: every dataset of both tabs with the settings of its last analysis, and every run of a single log. A row opens where it belongs, can be aborted while it runs, and deleted; deleting a dataset deletes the run that computed it, and the other way round.

items.dataset: Dataset: what cleaning left out and why, the descriptive statistics of every measure as ComFy's report prints them, and for a dataset computed from logs or nets the run times and input sizes. Both tables are folded until opened.
items.suitability: Suitability: Bartlett's test, the overall KMO and the MSA of every measure. The MSA filter removes measures in rounds, as ComFy does; any measure can be excluded by hand, all of them at once, or those a search finds. Where the analysis cannot run for too few observations, its message says what an observation is and leads to the measures or back to the data.
items.factors: Factors: the scree plot with the Kaiser line and parallel analysis, the count each criterion suggests, and the rotation.
items.loadings: Loadings: the rule that assigns measures to factors and the two thresholds in one row above the result, each rule explained in its tooltip; then a matrix (orange for negative loadings, faded where a loading does not count) or a card per dimension. Cross-loadings are ringed.
items.stability: Stability: Check stability under the loadings draws bootstrap samples of the rows (100, 200 or 500), refits each with the same measures, factor count and rotation, and shows for every measure the share of samples in which it keeps its factors. The seed is fixed, so a run can be repeated.
items.short_set: Short set: one measure per dimension, the one assigned to it with the highest purity, for reporting a few measures that do not repeat each other. Copy the short set puts them on the clipboard; a representative with a low stability should be read with care.
items.interpretation: Interpretation: optional, names for the factors, suggested by a language model only on request. It decides nothing. It needs an API key on the server; precomputed answers exist only once scripts/precompute_interpretations.py has been run. Without a key and without one stored for the settings, the list of steps says that it is not available here.
items.names: Names: press the title of a factor, on its card or at the head of its column, to name it; Enter keeps the name, Esc leaves it. The names appear in the loadings, the factor correlations, the list of steps and every download. They belong to the factor count, the rotation and the rule: changing one of them clears them, and the toast brings them back. With an interpretation, Use the suggested names takes its names over.
items.correlations: Correlation map: in Suitability, folded until opened. One cell for each pair of measures, orange for a negative correlation and the accent colour for a positive one, a pair with |r| ≥ 0.95 outlined, ordered by factor or clustered. Point at a cell or use the arrow keys to read the pair and its r; a table under the map has every value. The image icon downloads it like the other figures.
items.sheet: Fact sheet: press, or Enter on, the name of a measure wherever it stands to open a panel beside the page. It shows what the measure is (the description of the tool and the function of ComFy or feeed behind it, with a link to its source), a histogram of its values, its MSA and the round of the filter that removed it, its communality and uniqueness, its loadings, the five measures it correlates with most, and a button to exclude or include it. The left and right arrow keys page through the list you came from, Esc closes the panel and the focus goes back to the name.

export.title: Take the results into a paper
export.p1: The download menu in the page header has:

items.zip: Analysis (ZIP): the result, the matrix, the tables, report.tex, the figures, correlations.csv, the descriptive statistics, the run times, and a manifest with settings, versions and provenance.
items.report: LaTeX report: report.tex built like the report of ComFy, with the dimensions and the settings; compile it with latexmk -pdf, or run pdflatex twice, since long tables settle their widths in the second run.
items.print: Print view: the whole analysis on A4 pages, to print or save as PDF.
items.tables: The loadings as CSV or LaTeX, and the cleaned dataset as CSV.

export.p2: The image icon at the scree plot, the loadings and the correlation map downloads the figure as SVG, whose text stays text, or as PNG with 300 dpi: always light, at the text width of a CEUR paper, with the labels in the language of the app.
export.p3: The tag icon in the toolbar names the measures by the short codes of the papers, such as CNC or C_mag; the full name stays in the tooltip, and the figures, the report and the ZIP follow it.
export.p4: The link icon copies a link to the analysis of a published dataset with its settings.

compare.title: Compare miners
compare.p1: Compare miners puts the factor structures of several published datasets side by side, like Tab. 17 of Important Factors: which measures form which dimension for which miner. It is the tool Compare, at the right of the tabs, and two cards of Get started open it. The datasets and the rule are on the left, the result on the right; the notes on a column are a count in its header and one folded list below the table.

items.columns: Datasets: choose 2 to 8 of the miners of Important Factors; each is analysed with the settings of its paper. The first four are those of Tab. 17. A link can also ask for a dataset with a factor count of its own, such as 4 against 6 factors (Get started).
items.rule: Assignment rule: one rule for every dataset, Hair et al. as in Tab. 17 to begin with.
items.matrix: By measure: a row per measure, grouped by dimension, and above them n, the measures after the MSA filter, the KMO, the factors, the rotation and the variance explained per dataset. A tinted cell is in the dimension of its row; a ring marks a cross-loading, a dashed outline a measure the MSA filter removed.
items.dimensions: By dimension: a row per dataset with the measures of each dimension, laid out like Tab. 17.
items.pairs: Pairs: a square of the measures, each cell saying in how many of the datasets that analysed both the two share a dimension. It does not depend on how the dimensions are numbered.
items.export: The download menu has the matrix as CSV, the dimensions as a LaTeX table like Tab. 17, and both in a ZIP with a manifest.
items.own: Your own data: Compare the miners in the dataset step puts one column per miner, Compare in My datasets one column per dataset, and the pin icon in the loadings keeps the solution on screen (dataset, miner, factor count, rotation, rule), so that, say, the same dataset with 4 and with 6 factors sits side by side. Such a column starts from the settings saved with its dataset and lives in this session.

compare.p2: The factors of every analysis are numbered by the analysis, so they are matched first: the first dataset keeps its numbers, and the factors of every further one go to the dimension with which they share the most measures; where two are equally good, the more alike loadings decide. Tab. 17 renumbered its dimensions by hand, so a number can differ from the paper's, and a match that rests on one shared measure is a guess: the tooltip of a cell in the dimension view names the measures it rests on. How the measures are grouped within a dataset does not depend on the numbers.

compare.title: Compare factor structures
compare.subtitle: Which measures form which dimension for which miner, like Tab. 17 of Important Factors. Each column is an analysis: a published dataset with the settings of its paper, or one of your datasets with the settings saved with it. One assignment rule applies to all.
compare.subtitle_short: Which measures form which dimension for which miner.
compare.wait: The comparison is still being computed.
compare.stale: The table shows the previous selection; the update failed.
compare.link_invalid: Part of the link could not be used: a comparison takes {min} to {max} datasets, published or of this session, and one of the three rules. The rest of it is shown, or Tab. 17.

columns.label: Datasets
columns.min: A comparison needs at least {min} datasets.
columns.max: At most {max} datasets fit side by side.

compare.matrix_caption: Dimension of each measure per dataset under the rule {rule}: {columns}
compare.dimensions_caption: Measures of each dimension per dataset under the rule {rule}, laid out like Tab. 17
compare.alignment_note: D1, D2, … are the dimensions after matching: the first dataset keeps the numbers of its factors, and the factors of every further one are matched to them so that most of the measures they share get the same number. A number can differ from the paper's (Tab. 17 was renumbered by hand); how the measures are grouped within a dataset does not depend on it.
compare.codes_more: Names the measures by the codes of the papers, such as CNC or dens, in the tables and the LaTeX table. The full name stays in the tooltip.
compare.link_more: Copy a link that opens this comparison: the datasets and the rule

help.names: The names you gave the factors of this solution of your own dataset, factor by factor; a factor without a name is left out. The dimensions are matched across the analyses, the names stay with each analysis.
help.columns: Each tile is an analysis: a published dataset with the settings of its paper, or one of your datasets with the settings saved with it, pinned in the loadings step or chosen in My datasets. Choose {min} to {max}. The leftmost one keeps the numbers of its factors.
help.result: The dimensions of every dataset under the chosen rule. The factors of the datasets are matched so that most shared measures get the same number; where two matches are equally good, the more alike loadings decide.
help.n: Observations: the nets of the dataset, one per log.
help.measures: The measures left after cleaning and the MSA filter, of those in the dataset.
help.kmo: The overall measure of sampling adequacy (Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin) of the measures that are left.
help.factors: The number of factors, as the settings of the column fix it: those of the paper, or those saved with your dataset or pinned with it.
help.variance: The share of the variance of the measures that the factors explain together.
